title: Nine thousand tokens, four fields
spec: M10 · project, filter, summarize — and shape the failures too
intro: get_debtor_history returns everything the registry knows. The risk rule reads four fields. 93.6% of that tool result is paying rent in the context window to be ignored — and it is not free, because it changes the answer.

provenance.source: a narrated UCC risk agent's tool-result shaping; field-level token counts, verdicts and prices are plausible inventions, not measurements

foot: The layer this walks is M10's Shaping a Tool Result — shape_history(), projecting to used fields, filtering to active filings, truncating with a count, and giving errors a shape as well.

steps.title: The tool returns everything it has
narrative: The risk agent asks for a debtor's filing history. The registry API answers the way storage APIs answer: a pagination envelope wrapping 30 filings, each carrying about 40 fields — the collateral clause in full, the raw OCR text, a page-image reference, a clerk record, a checksum. 9,240 tokens land in the window.

The risk rule that consumes this reads four things: filing type, status, secured party, filed date. Everything else is passing through because it happened to be in the response, which is the default that ships in most pipelines.

The verdict comes back MEDIUM, and reruns of the identical call move between MEDIUM and LOW. That instability is the tell — the three active liens are three rows among thirty, and the other twenty-seven all say terminated.
steps.youDo: Print len(tokenize(tool_result)) next to the list of fields your downstream code actually reads. The gap is your shaping budget.

Risk: MEDIUM. The debtor has an extensive filing history, most of it resolved.

steps.title: Which tokens did the decision use?
narrative: Audit the response field by field across all thirty rows. Raw OCR text is 4,050 tokens. The full collateral clauses are 2,190. The remaining thirty-three fields — clerk, checksum, page-image reference, jurisdiction codes, the envelope itself — are 2,410 between them.

The four fields the risk rule reads, plus the filing ID needed to cite anything, come to 590 tokens across all thirty filings. That is 6.4% of the tool result. The other 93.6% is not merely wasted money; it is 8,650 tokens of plausible, on-topic text competing for attention with the five hundred that matter.

This is the specific reason the tool result is usually the largest low-value layer in an agent's window. Retrieved documents were at least selected for the query. A tool response was selected by whoever designed the table.
steps.claudeSays: The raw OCR block repeats each filing's text a second time in a noisier form. I have no way to know it is a duplicate, so I read it as thirty more documents.

steps.title: The shaped result carries the same facts
narrative: Between the tool and the window sits a layer you own. shape_history() projects to the five fields, filters to status == "active", sorts by recency, truncates past the top five with an explicit +N older active count, and prepends a one-line rollup so the terminated history is not lost, just not enumerated.

The result is 310 tokens. The verdict changes from an unstable MEDIUM to a stable HIGH, cited to three filing IDs — because the three active liens are no longer three rows in thirty. Same facts, fewer tokens, and the answer moved because the signal stopped being diluted.
Cost per call goes from $0.0416 to $0.0149. The shaping is 30 lines of Python that run before the model is called at all.
steps.youDo: Write the shaper as a pure function of the raw response and unit-test it. It is ordinary code, not prompt work, and it is the highest-leverage thirty lines in most agents.

terminal.text: Risk: HIGH — 2 new liens in 2024. Cites 2024-FL-0019988, 2024-FL-0012345, 2022-FL-0044120. Stable across 5 reruns.

steps.title: Two ways to shape it wrong
narrative: Shaping is a decision, so it can be decided badly. Six weeks later a commit drops status from USED_FIELDS — it is the same value on every row that survives the filter, so it looks redundant, and it saves 60 tokens a call. It is redundant right up until someone widens the filter to include terminated filings for a lookback report. Then the model sees five filings with no status field and calls a fully-discharged debtor HIGH risk. Sixty tokens saved, a wrong credit decision shipped.

The second failure is the one nobody shapes at all: the error path. The registry rate-limits, the client returns a 429 with a 400-token HTML body, and that body goes into the window unshaped. The model reads a page of markup, finds no filings in it, and reports "no liens found" — a false clean, which in a credit pipeline is the most expensive output the system can produce.

Shaped, the same failure is fourteen tokens and unambiguous: {"error": "rate_limited", "retry_after_s": 30, "filings": null}. The model says it cannot assess and the call is retried. An empty result needs the same treatment — "no prior filings found" is a fact, and a bare [] is an ambiguity.
steps.youDo: Feed your agent a rate-limit response, a 500, and an empty result set. If any of the three produces a confident answer instead of a refusal, your error path is unshaped.

⛔ a rate limit was reported to the credit committee as a clean debtor

view.text: A tool result is context you design, not data you dump. Project to the fields the decision reads, filter to the rows it reads, keep a rollup so nothing is silently lost, and keep the identifiers so the model can cite. Then shape the failures with the same care — an unshaped error does not degrade the answer, it replaces it with a confident wrong one.
